claim: Loss-of-function Parkin mutations lead to early-onset of Parkinson's disease.
source: Loss-of-function Parkin mutations lead to early-onset of Parkinson's disease.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Parkin is an auto-inhibited ubiquitin E3 ligase activated by dual phosphorylation of its ubiquitin-like (Ubl) domain and ubiquitin by the PINK1 kinase.
source: Parkin is an auto-inhibited ubiquitin E3 ligase activated by dual phosphorylation of its ubiquitin-like (Ubl) domain and ubiquitin by the PINK1 kinase.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations in the introduction.

claim: Phosphorylated Parkin can complex with native Parkin, leading to the activation of autoinhibited native Parkin in trans.
source: We show that phosphorylated Parkin can complex with native Parkin, leading to the activation of autoinhibited native Parkin in trans.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated through biophysical assays and ubiquitination assays shown in Figure 5.

claim: The activator element (ACT) of Parkin is required to maintain the enzyme kinetics.
source: We show that the activator element (ACT) of Parkin is required to maintain the enzyme kinetics, and the removal of ACT slows the enzyme catalysis.
evidence: This is demonstrated through ubiquitination assays comparing Parkin and Parkin ΔACT shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The removal of ACT slows the enzyme catalysis.
source: We show that the activator element (ACT) of Parkin is required to maintain the enzyme kinetics, and the removal of ACT slows the enzyme catalysis.
evidence: This is demonstrated through time-course ubiquitination assays shown in Figure 7C.

claim: ACT can activate Parkin in trans but less efficiently than when present in the cis molecule.
source: We also demonstrate that ACT can activate Parkin in trans but less efficiently than when present in the cis molecule.
evidence: This is demonstrated through ubiquitination assays comparing different pUbl constructs shown in Figure 8.

claim: The crystal structure reveals a donor ubiquitin binding pocket in the linker connecting REP and RING2, which plays a crucial role in Parkin activity.
source: Furthermore, the crystal structure reveals a donor ubiquitin binding pocket in the linker connecting REP and RING2, which plays a crucial role in Parkin activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated through crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 9 and validated through mutagenesis and binding assays.

claim: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra leading to motor defects.
source: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra leading to motor defects.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Mutations in PARK2 (Parkin) and PARK6 (PINK1) cause early-onset autosomal recessive juvenile parkinsonism (ARJP).
source: Mutations in several genes, such as PARK2 (Parkin) and PARK6 (PINK1, PTEN-induced kinase 1), cause early-onset autosomal recessive juvenile parkinsonism (ARJP).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Bonifati et al., 2002; Kitada et al., 1998; Valente et al., 2004).

claim: Parkin and PINK1 function together in a common mitochondrial homeostasis pathway in which damaged mitochondria are cleared by autophagy (mitophagy).
source: Parkin and PINK1 function together in a common mitochondrial homeostasis pathway in which damaged mitochondria are cleared by autophagy (mitophagy; Bonifati et al., 2002; Martin et al., 2011; Kitada et al., 1998; Valente et al., 2004; Chung et al., 2016; Exner et al., 2012; Narendra et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Parkin is an autoinhibited RBR family E3 ubiquitin ligase consisting of an N-terminal ubiquitin-like (Ubl) domain followed by four Zn2+ binding domains RING0, RING1, in-between-RING (IBR), and RING2.
source: Parkin is an autoinhibited RBR family E3 ubiquitin ligase (Chaugule et al., 2011) consisting of an N-terminal ubiquitin-like (Ubl) domain followed by four Zn2+ binding domains RING0, RING1, in-between-RING (IBR), and RING2 (Spratt et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Parkin is a cytosolic protein activated following mitochondrial stress, mediated by PINK1 phosphorylation of Serine 65 (S65) on ubiquitin.
source: Parkin is a cytosolic protein activated following mitochondrial stress, mediated by PINK1 phosphorylation of Serine 65 (S65) on ubiquitin.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Phosphorylation of ubiquitin enhances binding with Parkin and leads to the recruitment of Parkin to sites of damaged mitochondria.
source: Phosphorylation of ubiquitin enhances binding with Parkin and leads to the recruitment of Parkin to sites of damaged mitochondria (Kane et al., 2014; Kazlauskaite et al., 2014; Koyano et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: S65 of the Ubl domain of Parkin is phosphorylated by PINK1 on mitochondria.
source: On mitochondria, S65 of the Ubl domain of Parkin is phosphorylated by PINK1 (Kazlauskaite et al., 2014; Kondapalli et al., 2012; Shiba-Fukushima et al., 2014; Shiba-Fukushima et al., 2012), resulting in a fully active Parkin conformation.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Fully active Parkin attaches new ubiquitin molecules on mitochondrial proteins, which are phosphorylated by PINK1 to recruit more cytoplasmic Parkin to the mitochondria, resulting in a positive feedforward amplification cycle.
source: Fully active Parkin attaches new ubiquitin molecules on mitochondrial proteins, which are phosphorylated by PINK1 to recruit more cytoplasmic Parkin to the mitochondria, thus resulting in a positive feedforward amplification cycle (Ordureau et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Ubiquitination of mitochondrial proteins by Parkin leads to the recruitment of autophagy receptors required for mitophagy.
source: Ubiquitination of mitochondrial proteins by Parkin also leads to the recruitment of autophagy receptors required for mitophagy (Tanaka et al., 2010; Chan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Parkin binds to an E2, and ubiquitin is transferred from E2 onto the catalytic C431 residue (on RING2) of Parkin before ubiquitination of lysines on target substrates.
source: Like other RBR-family E3 ligases, Parkin binds to an E2, and ubiquitin is transferred from E2 onto the catalytic C431 residue (on RING2) of Parkin before ubiquitination of lysines on target substrates (Wenzel et al., 2011; Walden and Rittinger, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The E2 binding site on RING1 is blocked by the Ubl domain and the short repressor (REP) element.
source: The E2 binding site on RING1 is blocked by the Ubl domain and the short repressor (REP) element.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: C431 on RING2 is occluded by the RING0 domain of Parkin, which inhibits Parkin activity.
source: Furthermore, C431 on RING2 is occluded by the RING0 domain of Parkin, which inhibits Parkin activity (Chaugule et al., 2011; Riley et al., 2013; Trempe et al., 2013; Wauer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The phospho-Ubl domain binds within a basic patch (comprising K161, R163, and K211) on RING0 and displaces RING2 to expose C431 to activate Parkin.
source: The phospho-Ubl domain binds within a basic patch (comprising K161, R163, and K211) on RING0 and displaces RING2 to expose C431 to activate Parkin (Gladkova et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In the structure of phospho-Parkin with RING2 removed, an activating element (ACT, 101–109), which is present in the linker region (77-140) between Ubl and RING0 domains, binds on the RING0 interface.
source: In the structure of phospho-Parkin with RING2 removed, an activating element (ACT, 101–109), which is present in the linker region (77-140) between Ubl and RING0 domains, binds on the RING0 interface (Gladkova et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Mutations in the ACT negatively affect Parkin activity.
source: Mutations in the ACT are shown to affect Parkin activity negatively (Gladkova et al., 2018), suggesting their importance in Parkin regulation.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Phospho-ubiquitin (pUb) binds in a pocket between RING0 and RING1, and activates Parkin allosterically.
source: Phospho-ubiquitin (pUb) binds in a pocket between RING0 and RING1, and activates Parkin allosterically (Wauer et al., 2015; Sauvé et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: pUb binding results in the displacement of the IBR domain, and the straightening of helix-1 of the RING1 domain.
source: pUb binding results in the displacement of the IBR domain, and the straightening of helix-1 of the RING1 domain (Kumar et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Massive domain rearrangements have been proposed in the active state to allow the transfer of donor ubiquitin (bound between helix-1 and IBR) from E2 (on RING1) to C431 (on RING2) of Parkin.
source: Massive domain rearrangements have been proposed in the active state to allow the transfer of donor ubiquitin (bound between helix-1 and IBR) from E2 (on RING1) to C431 (on RING2) of Parkin (Gladkova et al., 2018; Kumar et al., 2017; Sauvé et al., 2018; Condos et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Ubl-linker (1-140) co-elutes with R0RBR (141-465) in native Parkin (3C, TEV) after treatment with 3C protease, suggesting a stronger interaction between Ubl and the Parkin core.
source: Furthermore, we noticed co-elution of Ubl-linker (1-140) with R0RBR (141-465) in native Parkin (3C, TEV) after treatment with 3C protease, suggesting a stronger interaction between Ubl and the Parkin core (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through SEC assay shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In phosphorylated Parkin (3C, TEV) treated with 3C, pUbl-linker (1-140) did not form a complex with R0RBR (141-465), suggesting a poor/no interaction between phospho-Ubl with the core of Parkin.
source: However, in phosphorylated Parkin (3C, TEV) treated with 3C, pUbl-linker (1-140) did not form a complex with R0RBR (141-465), suggesting a poor/no interaction between phospho-Ubl with the core of Parkin (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through SEC assay shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In native Parkin (3C, TEV) treated with TEV, RING2 (383-465) co-eluted with Parkin (1-382), suggesting a stronger interaction between RING2 and the Parkin core in the native Parkin.
source: Furthermore, in native Parkin (3C, TEV) treated with TEV, RING2 (383-465) co-eluted with Parkin (1-382), suggesting a stronger interaction between RING2 and the Parkin core in the native Parkin (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through SEC assay shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In phospho-Parkin (3C, TEV) treated with TEV, RING2 (383-465) eluted separately from the Parkin (1-382), suggesting that phosphorylation of the Ubl domain results in the displacement of the RING2 domain.
source: However, in phospho-Parkin (3C, TEV) treated with TEV, RING2 (383-465) eluted separately from the Parkin (1-382), suggesting that phosphorylation of the Ubl domain results in the displacement of the RING2 domain (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through SEC assay shown in Figure 1D.

claim: pUbl-linker (1-140) co-eluted with Parkin core (141-382) upon 3C treatment on fractions that were collected after TEV treatment on phospho-Parkin (3C, TEV) which led to the displacement of RING2 (383-465).
source: Interestingly, pUbl-linker (1-140) co-eluted with Parkin core (141-382) upon 3C treatment on fractions that were collected after TEV treatment on phospho-Parkin (3C, TEV) which led to the displacement of RING2 (383-465) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through sequential protease treatment and SEC assay shown in Figure 2A.

claim: RING2 (383-465) co-eluted with Parkin core (141-382) upon TEV treatment on fractions that were collected after 3C treatment on phospho-Parkin (3C, TEV) which led to the displacement of pUbl-linker (1-140).
source: Similarly, RING2 (383-465) co-eluted with Parkin core (141-382) upon TEV treatment on fractions that were collected after 3C treatment on phospho-Parkin (3C, TEV) which led to the displacement of pUbl-linker (1-140) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through sequential protease treatment and SEC assay shown in Figure 2B.

claim: pUbl and RING2 competitively bind on RING0.
source: This data confirmed that pUbl and RING2 competitively bind on RING0.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequential protease treatment experiments shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: The overall structure of pUbl-linker (1-140) depleted Parkin (141-465)-pUb complex showed similar conformation as seen in previously solved structures of Parkin in the autoinhibited state.
source: The overall structure of pUbl-linker (1-140) depleted Parkin (141-465)-pUb complex was determined at 3.3 Å (Table 1), and showed similar conformation as seen in previously solved structures of Parkin in the autoinhibited state (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The crystal structure showed RING2 bound to RING0, which confirmed that RING2 was only transiently displaced from the RING0 domain in phospho-Parkin and returned to its original position after removal of pUbl-linker.
source: The crystal structure showed RING2 bound to RING0, which confirmed that RING2 was only transiently displaced from the RING0 domain in phospho-Parkin and returned to its original position after removal of pUbl-linker (Figure 2C), further confirming our SEC data (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 2C and SEC data in Figure 2B.

claim: pUbl and RING2 exist in a dynamic state in phospho-Parkin (pUbl binding<->RING2 open<->pUbl displaced<->RING2 closed), and compete for binding on RING0.
source: Overall, this data suggested that pUbl and RING2 exist in a dynamic state in phospho-Parkin (pUbl binding<->RING2 open<->pUbl displaced<->RING2 closed), and compete for binding on RING0.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data of SEC assays and crystal structure analysis.

claim: pUbl-linker (1-140) remained flexible in phospho-Parkin K211N (3C, TEV) and eluted separately from Parkin core (141-465) on SEC.
source: Interestingly, similar to phospho-Parkin (3C, TEV) (Figure 2C), pUbl-linker (1-140) remained flexible in phospho-Parkin K211N (3C, TEV) and eluted separately from Parkin core (141-465) on SEC (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through SEC assay shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The binding of pUbl with the basic patch on RING0 domain may not be the driving force for pUbl displacement.
source: This data suggests that the binding of pUbl with the basic patch on RING0 domain may not be the driving force for pUbl displacement.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that K211N mutation does not prevent pUbl displacement.

claim: K211N resulted in stabilization of the RING2 (383-465) domain on phospho-Parkin K211N (1-382) upon TEV treatment, and the two fragments co-eluted on SEC.
source: K211N resulted in stabilization of the RING2 (383-465) domain on phospho-Parkin K211N (1-382) upon TEV treatment, and the two fragments co-eluted on SEC (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through SEC assay shown in Figure 3A.

claim: RING2 displacement, not Ubl displacement, is a major cause of Parkin activation.
source: Although pUbl was displaced in phospho-Parkin K211N, Parkin activity was drastically reduced (Figure 3B), suggesting RING2 displacement, not Ubl displacement, is a major cause of Parkin activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: No complex formation between phospho-Parkin K211N and ΔUbl-Parkin was seen on SEC.
source: However, no complex formation between phospho-Parkin K211N and ΔUbl-Parkin was seen on SEC (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through SEC assay shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ITC did not show any detectable interaction between phospho-Parkin K211N and ΔUbl-Parkin.
source: We next validated this finding using isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC), which did not show any detectable interaction between phospho-Parkin K211N and ΔUbl-Parkin (Figure 4A), consistent with previously published reports.
evidence: This is demonstrated through ITC assay shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Incubation of phospho-Parkin K211N with untethered ΔUbl-Parkin (TEV) led to the displacement of RING2 (383-465) from ΔUbl-Parkin (77-382), and a stable trans-complex between phospho-Parkin K211N and ΔUbl-Parkin (77-382) by SEC analysis.
source: Incubation of phospho-Parkin K211N with untethered ΔUbl-Parkin (TEV) led to the displacement of RING2 (383-465) from ΔUbl-Parkin (77-382), and a stable trans-complex between phospho-Parkin K211N and ΔUbl-Parkin (77-382) by SEC analysis (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through SEC assay shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The ITC showed a strong affinity (Kd = 1.1 ± 0.3 µM) between phospho-Parkin K211N and untethered ΔUbl-Parkin (TEV).
source: The ITC showed a strong affinity (Kd = 1.1 ± 0.3 µM) between phospho-Parkin K211N and untethered ΔUbl-Parkin (TEV; Figure 4B), which further supported the SEC data.
evidence: This is demonstrated through ITC assay shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In the crystal structure, the pUbl domain from the donor molecule (phospho-Parkin K211N (3C)) was bound to the basic patch of RING0 on the acceptor molecule (untethered R0RBR (TEV)) in trans.
source: In the crystal structure, the pUbl domain from the donor molecule (phospho-Parkin K211N (3C)) was bound to the basic patch of RING0 on the acceptor molecule (untethered R0RBR (TEV)) (Figure 4D) in trans.
evidence: This is demonstrated through crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Phospho-Parkin formed a stable complex with ΔUbl-Parkin (77-382) and RING2 (383-465) was displaced from untethered ΔUbl-Parkin (TEV).
source: Interestingly, phospho-Parkin formed a stable complex with ΔUbl-Parkin (77-382) and RING2 (383-465) was displaced from untethered ΔUbl-Parkin (TEV) (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), similar to the interaction between phospho-Parkin K211N and untethered ΔUbl-Parkin (TEV).
evidence: This is demonstrated through SEC assay shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Untethered WT-Parkin (TEV) formed a complex with phospho-Parkin, and resulted in the removal of RING2 (383-465) from WT-Parkin (1-382).
source: Similar to untethered ΔUbl-Parkin (TEV), untethered WT-Parkin (TEV) formed a complex with phospho-Parkin, and resulted in the removal of RING2 (383-465) from WT-Parkin (1-382) (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through SEC assay shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Untethered Parkin K211N (TEV) failed to form the complex with phospho-Parkin.
source: However, unlike untethered WT-Parkin (TEV), untethered Parkin K211N (TEV) failed to form the complex with phospho-Parkin (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through SEC assay shown in Figure 5C.

claim: MALS analysis confirmed complex formation between phospho-Parkin (Observed M. W.=53 ± 2 Kda) and untethered WT-Parkin (TEV) (Observed M. W.=52 ± 3 Kda) with an observed molecular weight of 94 ± 3 Kda.
source: MALS analysis further confirmed complex (Phospho-Parkin and WT-Parkin (1-382), Observed M. W.=94 ± 3 Kda) formation between phospho-Parkin (Observed M. W.=53 ± 2 Kda) and untethered WT-Parkin (TEV) (Observed M. W.=52 ± 3 Kda) (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through SEC-MALS analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: WT-Parkin ubiquitination/autoubiquitination activity was increased with increasing concentrations of phospho-Parkin T270R/C431A.
source: Interestingly, we observed that WT-Parkin ubiquitination/autoubiquitination activity was increased with increasing concentrations of phospho-Parkin T270R/C431A (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through ubiquitination assay shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Unlike pUb, pUbl did not enhance Parkin phosphorylation by PINK1.
source: However, unlike pUb, pUbl did not enhance Parkin phosphorylation by PINK1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D), confirming that pUbl and pUb binding lead to unique conformational changes in Parkin.
evidence: This is demonstrated through Phos-Tag analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Co-expression of mCherry-tagged-Parkin WT with GFP-Parkin C431F enabled GFP-Parkin C431F recruitment to the mitochondria.
source: We observed that co-expression of mCherry-tagged-Parkin WT with GFP-Parkin C431F enabled GFP-Parkin C431F recruitment to the mitochondria, similar to a previous study (Lazarou et al., 2013; Figure 6A and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 6A and quantified in Figure 6D.

claim: Mutation of the pUb binding pocket in the RING1 completely abolished recruitment of the double mutant GFP-Parkin C431F/H302 to the mitochondria when co-expressed with mCherry-tagged-Parkin WT.
source: Under these assay conditions, we strikingly observed that mutation of the pUb binding pocket in the RING1 completely abolished recruitment of the double mutant GFP-Parkin C431F/H302 to the mitochondria when co-expressed with mCherry-tagged-Parkin WT (Figure 6B and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 6B and quantified in Figure 6D.

claim: Mutation of the RING0 binding pocket produced a moderate defect in recruitment of the double mutant GFP-Parkin C431F/K211N to the mitochondria when co-expressed with mCherry-tagged-Parkin WT.
source: In line with this, mutation of the RING0 binding pocket produced a moderate defect in recruitment of the double mutant GFP-Parkin C431F/K211N to the mitochondria when co-expressed with mCherry-tagged-Parkin WT (Figure 6C and D), suggesting that the transient interaction between pUbl and RING0 of Parkin in trans acts in concert with pUb binding to RING1 pocket for optimal Parkin recruitment to sites of mitochondrial damage (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 6C and quantified in Figure 6D.

claim: Co-expression of GFP-Parkin C431F or GFP-Parkin C431F/K211N or GFP-Parkin C431F/H302A with the non-phosphorylatable mCherry-tagged-Parkin S65A failed to rescue recruitment to the mitochondria.
source: Furthermore, co-expression of GFP-Parkin C431F or GFP-Parkin C431F/K211N or GFP-Parkin C431F/H302A with the non-phosphorylatable mCherry-tagged-Parkin S65A failed to rescue recruitment to the mitochondria (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 6A-C and quantified in Figure 6D.

claim: Deletion of ACT did not affect the complex formation with E2~Ub, as phospho-Parkin ∆ACT co-eluted with pUb and E2~Ub.
source: Interestingly, deletion of the ACT did not affect the complex formation with E2~Ub, as phospho-Parkin ∆ACT co-eluted with pUb and E2~Ub (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through SEC assay shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Phospho-Parkin ∆ACT (TEV) after treatment with TEV resulted in a shift where RING2 (383-465) was displaced from the Parkin core (1–382, ∆ACT), resulting in the elution of two fragments of Parkin separately on SEC.
source: We observed that phospho-Parkin ∆ACT (TEV) after treatment with TEV resulted in a shift where RING2 (383-465) was displaced from the Parkin core (1–382, ∆ACT), resulting in the elution of two fragments of Parkin separately on SEC (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through SEC assay shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The deletion of ACT slowed the kinetics of Parkin activity, doubling the time for phospho-Parkin ∆ACT to reach a similar level of activity as phospho-Parkin.
source: We observed that the deletion of ACT slowed the kinetics of Parkin activity, doubling the time for phospho-Parkin ∆ACT to reach a similar level of activity as phospho-Parkin (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through time-course ubiquitination assay shown in Figure 7C.

claim: In the previous structure of phospho-Parkin (1-382)-pUb complex (PDBID: 6GLC), the ACT region was clearly shown to occupy the hydrophobic pocket on RING0.
source: In the previous structure of phospho-Parkin (1-382)-pUb complex (PDBID: 6GLC), the ACT region was clearly shown to occupy the hydrophobic pocket on RING0 (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of previously published crystal structure.

claim: No density of the ACT region was observed in the ternary trans-complex structure of phospho-Parkin (1–140+141-382 + pUb).
source: However, we did not see any density of the ACT region in the ternary trans-complex structure of phospho-Parkin (1–140+141-382 + pUb) (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: In the ternary trans-complex structure of phospho-Parkin, K48 of the pUbl domain occupied the same pocket that R104 of the ACT region occupied in the structure of phospho-Parkin-pUb complex.
source: Interestingly, we observed that in the ternary trans-complex structure of phospho-Parkin, K48 of the pUbl domain occupied the same pocket that R104 of the ACT region occupied in the structure of phospho-Parkin-pUb complex (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: In the structure of the ternary trans-complex of phospho-Parkin with cis ACT, electron density of the ACT region was observed.
source: Interestingly, in the structure of the ternary trans-complex of phospho-Parkin with cis ACT, we could observe the electron density of the ACT region (Figure 8C, Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claim: K48, which occupied the ACT region in the ternary trans-complex structure of phospho-Parkin with trans ACT, was disordered in the ternary trans-complex structure of phospho-Parkin with cis ACT.
source: Furthermore, K48, which occupied the ACT region in the ternary trans-complex structure of phospho-Parkin with trans ACT, was disordered in the ternary trans-complex structure of phospho-Parkin with cis ACT, similar to what was seen previously in the phospho-Parkin structure (Figure 8A and C, Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 8A and 8C.

claim: The presence of a linker (77-140) containing ACT in ∆Ubl-Parkin (77-465) made it more active compared to R0RBR (141-465).
source: The presence of a linker (77-140) containing ACT in ∆Ubl-Parkin (77-465) made it more active compared to R0RBR (141-465) (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through ubiquitination assay shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: pUbl (1-76) efficiently activated ∆Ubl-Parkin (77-465); however, R0RBR (141-465) activation by pUbl (1-76) was very poor.
source: We observed that pUbl (1-76) efficiently activated ∆Ubl-Parkin (77-465); however, R0RBR (141-465) activation by pUbl (1-76) was very poor (Figure 8D, Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through ubiquitination assay shown in Figure 8D.

claim: ∆Ubl-Parkin activation was not affected by the linker (77-140) or ACT region in trans.
source: Interestingly, ubiquitination assays performed using increasing concentrations of pUbl (1-76) or pUbl-linker (1-140), or pUbl-linker-∆ACT (1–140, ∆101–109) showed that ∆Ubl-Parkin activation was not affected by the linker (77-140) or ACT region in trans (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through ubiquitination assay shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Compared to pUbl (1-76), pUbl-linker (1-140) showed better activation of R0RBR (141-465).
source: However, compared to pUbl (1-76), pUbl-linker (1-140) showed better activation of R0RBR (141-465) (Figure 8F, Figure 8—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through ubiquitination assay shown in Figure 8F.

claim: In contrast to pUbl-linker (1-140), pUbl-linker-∆ACT (1–140, ∆101–109) showed poor activation of R0RBR (141-465) which was similar to pUbl (1-76).
source: Also, in contrast to pUbl-linker (1-140), pUbl-linker-∆ACT (1–140, ∆101–109) showed poor activation of R0RBR (141-465) which was similar to pUbl (1-76) (Figure 8F, Figure 8—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through ubiquitination assay shown in Figure 8F.

claim: ACT can be complemented in trans; however, ACT is more efficient in cis.
source: Overall, our data suggested that ACT can be complemented in trans; however, ACT is more efficient in cis.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data of crystal structures and ubiquitination assays shown in Figure 8.

claim: In the crystal structure of R0RBR (R163D/K211N)-pUb complex, one molecule of Parkin showed electron density of the linker (408-415) region of Parkin.
source: In the crystal structure of R0RBR (R163D/K211N)-pUb complex, out of two molecules of Parkin in the asymmetric unit, one molecule of Parkin showed nice electron density of the linker (408-415) region of Parkin (Figure 9A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 9A and B.

claim: Conformational changes were observed in the linker (408-415) region in the structure of the R0RBR (R163D/K211N)-pUb complex when compared to the previously solved apo R0RBR structure (PDBID: 4I1H).
source: We further noticed conformational changes in the linker (408-415) region in the structure of the R0RBR (R163D/K211N)-pUb complex when compared to the previously solved apo R0RBR structure (PDBID: 4I1H) (Figure 9—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through crystal structure comparison shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Interactions were observed between the linker (408-415) of Parkin and pUb from the neighboring molecule of the asymmetric unit.
source: Interestingly, we noticed interactions between the linker (408-415) of Parkin and pUb from the neighboring molecule of the asymmetric unit (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The core of interactions between the Parkin linker and ubiquitin was mediated by I411, which was involved in hydrophobic interactions with the hydrophobic pocket of ubiquitin.
source: The core of interactions between the Parkin linker and ubiquitin was mediated by I411, which was involved in hydrophobic interactions with the hydrophobic pocket of ubiquitin (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 9C.

claim: In contrast to WT-Parkin, E409A and H422A drastically reduced Parkin activity, whilst I411A, T415N, and K416A resulted in the complete abolishment of Parkin activity.
source: In contrast to WT-Parkin, E409A and H422A drastically reduced Parkin activity, whilst I411A, T415N, and K416A resulted in the complete abolishment of Parkin activity (Figure 9E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through ubiquitination assay shown in Figure 9E.

claim: Unlike phospho-Parkin, which formed a stable complex with E2~Ubdon on SEC and co-eluted with E2~Ubdon and phospho-ubiquitin, phospho-Parkin I411A did not show interaction with E2~Ubdon.
source: Interestingly, unlike phospho-Parkin, which formed a stable complex with E2~Ubdon on SEC and co-eluted with E2~Ubdon and phospho-ubiquitin (Figure 9F), phospho-Parkin I411A did not show interaction with E2~Ubdon (Figure 9F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through SEC assay shown in Figure 9F.

claim: Unlike phospho-Parkin, phospho-Parkin I411A did not react with Ub-VS.
source: Furthermore, the SEC data was confirmed by ubiquitin-vinyl sulfone (Ub-VS) assay where unlike phospho-Parkin, phospho-Parkin I411A did not react with Ub-VS (Figure 9—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through Ub-VS assay shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Compared to native ubiquitin, ubiquitin mutants (L71A or L73A) showed a loss of Parkin activity.
source: Compared to native ubiquitin, ubiquitin mutants showed a loss of Parkin activity (Figure 9—figure supplement 2C) which nicely corroborated with our data.
evidence: This is demonstrated through ubiquitination assay shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The linker region between REP and RING2 interacts with donor ubiquitin and plays a crucial role in Parkin function.
source: Overall, our data showed that the linker region between REP and RING2 interacts with donor ubiquitin and plays a crucial role in Parkin function.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data of crystal structure analysis, mutagenesis, and binding assays shown in Figure 9.

claim: Previous cellular data co-expressing WT-Parkin and mutant Parkin constructs suggested the self-association of Parkin molecules after PINK1 activation at sites of damaged mitochondria.
source: Previous cellular data co-expressing WT-Parkin and mutant Parkin constructs suggested the self-association of Parkin molecules after PINK1 activation at sites of damaged mitochondria (Lazarou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Structural studies to understand the Parkin activation mechanism in the last decade have not captured any dimerization of Parkin in vitro.
source: Furthermore, structural studies to understand the Parkin activation mechanism in the last decade have not captured any dimerization of Parkin in vitro (Wenzel et al., 2011; Walden and Rittinger, 2018; Riley et al., 2013; Trempe et al., 2013; Wauer and Komander, 2013; Gladkova et al., 2018; Wauer et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2015; Sauvé et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2017; Sauvé et al., 2018; Condos et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The phospho-Ubl (pUbl) domain transiently binds to the basic patch on RING0 and competes with the RING2 domain.
source: Our data suggest that the phospho-Ubl (pUbl) domain transiently binds to the basic patch on RING0 and competes with the RING2 domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data of SEC assays and crystal structures shown in Figure 2.

claim: The presence of RING2 restricts the binding of pUbl with the Parkin core.
source: In addition to the previous observation that pUbl binding results in RING2 displacement, our new data show that the presence of RING2 restricts the binding of pUbl with the Parkin core, which establishes the competitive mode of interaction between RING2 and pUbl.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data of SEC assays shown in Figure 2 and Figure 4.

claim: RING2 is displaced transiently during the activation process and returns to its closed state after the removal of the pUbl domain from phospho-Parkin.
source: The crystal structure of pUbl-linker (1-140) depleted Parkin (141-465)-pUb complex and supporting data show that RING2 is displaced transiently during the activation process and returns to its closed state after the removal of the pUbl domain from phospho-Parkin, suggesting dynamic nature of conformational changes during Parkin activation.
evidence: This is demonstrated through crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 2C and SEC data in Figure 2B.

claim: Parkin dimerization is mediated by interactions between pUbl and the basic patch on the RING0 domain in trans.
source: Furthermore, we report Parkin dimerization, mediated by interactions between pUbl and the basic patch on the RING0 domain in trans.
evidence: This is demonstrated through SEC, ITC, SEC-MALS, and crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 4 and Figure 5.

claim: Phospho-Parkin activates autoinhibited Parkin in trans, suggesting an additional feedforward mechanism of Parkin activation.
source: We also demonstrate that phospho-Parkin activates autoinhibited Parkin in trans, suggesting an additional feedforward mechanism of Parkin activation.
evidence: This is demonstrated through ubiquitination assay shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Similar to phospho-Ubl, ACT can also work in trans, although ACT is more efficient in cis.
source: We show that similar to phospho-Ubl, ACT can also work in trans, although ACT is more efficient in cis.
evidence: This is demonstrated through crystal structures and ubiquitination assays shown in Figure 8.

claim: A new donor ubiquitin binding site exists in the linker region (408-415) between the REP element and RING2, which plays a crucial role in Parkin activity.
source: Furthermore, using X-ray crystallography and supporting experiments, we have characterized a new donor ubiquitin binding site in the linker region (408-415) between the REP element and RING2, which plays a crucial role in Parkin activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated through crystal structure analysis and mutagenesis shown in Figure 9.

claim: The inclusion of protease sites (HRV 3C and TEV) did not affect the protein folding or function of Parkin.
source: First, we tested the ubiquitination activity of Parkin (3C, TEV) to ensure that the inclusion of protease sites did not affect the protein folding or function, which is confirmed by the similar activity of Parkin (3C, TEV) as of the native Parkin construct (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated through ubiquitination assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The ternary trans-complex of phospho-Parkin (1–140+141-382 + pUb) structure was solved at 1.92 Å.
source: The crystal structure of the ternary trans-complex of phospho-Parkin (pUbl-linker (1-140)+R0RB (141-382)+pUb) was solved at 1.92 Å (Table 1), which further confirmed trans-complex formation between Parkin molecules (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated through crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 4D and Table 1.

claim: The ternary trans-complex of phospho-Parkin with cis ACT (1–76+77-382 + pUb) was crystallized, and structure was determined at 2.6 Å.
source: The ternary trans-complex of phospho-Parkin (1–76+77-382 + pUb) with cis ACT was crystallized, and structure was determined at 2.6 Å (Table 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 8C and Table 1.

claim: The overall structure of pUbl-linker (1-140) depleted Parkin (141-465)-pUb complex was determined at 3.3 Å.
source: The overall structure of pUbl-linker (1-140) depleted Parkin (141-465)-pUb complex was determined at 3.3 Å (Table 1), and showed similar conformation as seen in previously solved structures of Parkin in the autoinhibited state (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 2C and Table 1.

claim: The overall structure of the pUbl-linker (1-140) depleted Parkin R163D/K211N/Q347C (141-465)-pUb complex was similar to the autoinhibited structure wherein RING2 was bound on RING0 and REP element was bound on RING1.
source: The overall structure of the pUbl-linker (1-140) depleted Parkin R163D/K211N/Q347C (141-465)-pUb complex (hereafter R0RBR R163D/K211N-pUb complex) was similar to the autoinhibited structure wherein RING2 was bound on RING0 and REP element was bound on RING1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Hydrophobic nature at the corresponding position of I411 on Parkin is conserved among various RBRs except RNF216.
source: Further inspection revealed that although the linker region of Parkin is not conserved across different members of RBR family E3-ligases (Figure 9—figure supplement 1D), hydrophobic nature at the corresponding position of I411 on Parkin is conserved among various RBRs except RNF216 (Figure 9—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through sequence alignment shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The crystal structures of HOIP, HOIL, HHARI, and RNF216 solved with E2~Ub showed interactions between the linker region and donor ubiquitin (Ubdon).
source: Also, the crystal structures of HOIP, HOIL, HHARI, and RNF216 solved with E2~Ub (Lechtenberg et al., 2016; Horn-Ghetko et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2023) showed interactions between the linker region and donor ubiquitin (Ubdon) (Figure 9—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of previously published crystal structures.
